summary:
Argentina's Law 26.743 remains one of the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. It was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and promulgated on 24 May 2012. It allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned the courts to intervene. The outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours; Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026 and described them as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed on 4 April 2025 by the Washington Blade, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán, who was stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is not applied in the case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
The 2025 decrees narrow practice under Law 26.743 without amending the statute: the law's core entitlement to legal gender change without medical or judicial prerequisites remains in force, while the restrictions target minors and the treatment of transgender prisoners.

The 2020 removal of the travesticidio aggravating circumstance from the Sacayán prosecution, and the Supreme Court's decision in April 2025 not to restore it, set the current position on how gender-motivated killings are charged, even as the underlying murder conviction and life sentence were upheld.

The record hate-crime count for 2025 coincides with the period in which activists reported heightened vulnerability, so the deterioration recorded by Outright International in March 2026 aligns with the violence data reported for the preceding year.

Argentina's position as a regional pioneer, on marriage equality in 2010 and on gender recognition in 2012, provides the benchmark against which the current trajectory is measured by international observers.
localsOnly:
Anti-discrimination protections are available to residents through national legislation as well as through the laws of individual provinces, so the applicable provision depends on where in the country a person lives.

The February 2025 decree on the housing of transgender people in prison governs the placement of trans detainees within the national prison system, and affects people serving sentences rather than visitors.

Community organisations in Buenos Aires named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins are among the groups that report on and respond to violence against trans people locally.

Outright International's March 2026 overview flags the registration of organisations as a negative area, which bears on the operation of trans and LGBTI+ groups based in the country.

Marriage equality has been available nationwide since 2010.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the court challenge to the February 2025 decree on minors is unresolved in the sources available here; whether the decree has been suspended, upheld or struck down is not established.

The 227 hate crimes recorded for 2025 come from a single monitoring body, the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio. Its geographic coverage, reporting methodology and the proportion of incidents that resulted in criminal charges are not sourced here.

No sourced information in this inventory addresses entry or visa screening, passport or identity-document markers for transgender travellers, or access to gender-affirming care for adults. Those areas are not covered rather than confirmed as unproblematic.

A Buenos Aires safety guide updated on 28 May 2026 offers a first-person account of walking in the capital at all hours, aimed at gay visitors. It contains no trans-specific legal finding and is not treated as evidence of conditions nationwide.

Whether the prison-housing decree has been implemented, and how it is applied in practice by the prison authority, is not sourced.
